text:
The hum had become Blackwood Bay’s new pulse, a low, thrumming current beneath the usual creak of old wood and the distant sigh of the bay. Locals chalked it up to the aging power grid, or the shifting continental plates, or simply the sound of a town settling into its bones. David Vance knew better. He’d lived in enough places to know what silence sounded like, and this wasn’t it. This was something else, a resonant frequency that vibrated not just through the floorboards of the Black Cat Diner, but through his teeth.

It had started subtly, a mere whisper in the background, like distant machinery. But in the last week, it had gained weight, a pressure behind the ears, a phantom static fuzzing the edges of his hearing. He’d tried to record it, holding his phone aloft like a divining rod, but the playback only offered the usual ambient noise. Yet, the hum persisted, a constant reminder of something unseen and unheard by most, a secret conversation Blackwood Bay was having with itself.

He ran a hand through his perpetually disheveled hair, pushing aside the cold coffee. The waitress, a woman named Martha who had seen too many tourists and not enough sunshine, slid his check across the Formica. She didn’t even seem to register the low vibration that made the sugar dispenser shiver faintly. For David, it was a siren, a quiet, insistent call that something was stirring beneath the surface, something the town was willing to label as mundane, a glitch in the background noise of life. He wondered what kind of hoax the truth would turn out to be.
